questions.q: C++ is best described as:
Which of the following features is present in C++ but not in standard C?
C is to procedural programming as C++ primarily adds support for:
Which keyword used for input/output in C++ is NOT present in C?
Function overloading, a feature not found in standard C, is supported in C++ because C++ uses:
options: Name mangling to distinguish functions by signature

questions.q: Which statement about C and C++ is true?
options: C++ is a strict subset of C
C++ is generally considered a superset of C with added OOP features
C and C++ have identical syntax rules
C supports classes while C++ does not

questions.q: A namespace in C++ is primarily used to:
Which keyword is used to define a namespace?
The std namespace contains:
options: The C++ Standard Library entities like cout, cin, vector

questions.q: Which statement correctly brings all names from the std namespace into scope?
The scope resolution operator used to access a namespace member is:
Nested namespaces in C++ allow:
options: Namespaces to be declared inside other namespaces

questions.q: A reference variable in C++ must be:
options: Initialized at the time of declaration

questions.q: Unlike a pointer, a reference in C++:
options: Cannot be made to refer to another variable after initialization
Needs the & operator every time it is used

questions.q: Which symbol is used to declare a reference variable?
Pointers can be reassigned to point to different variables, whereas references:
options: Are bound to one variable for their lifetime
Cannot be used in function parameters

questions.q: Passing a variable by reference to a function allows the function to:
options: Create a completely independent copy always

questions.q: Which of the following is true about pointer arithmetic compared to references?
options: Reference arithmetic is allowed just like pointers
Pointer arithmetic is allowed, but reference arithmetic is not meaningful/allowed
Neither pointers nor references allow arithmetic

questions.q: A pointer variable, unlike a reference, can be:
options: Assigned NULL and reassigned to different addresses

questions.q: In C++, references are often preferred over pointers for function parameters because:
options: They provide a safer, cleaner syntax without needing dereferencing
They can be NULL and easily checked
They always create copies of large objects

questions.q: Function overloading in C++ means:
options: Defining multiple functions with the same name but different parameter lists
Defining multiple functions with the same name and same parameters
Using the same function in multiple files

questions.q: Two overloaded functions can differ in:
Which of the following is a valid example of function overloading?
options: int add(int a,int b); int add(int x,int y);

questions.q: Function overloading is resolved by the compiler at:
Overloading functions based solely on return type (with identical parameters) is:
options: Not allowed because it causes ambiguity

questions.q: Which term describes the process the compiler uses to select the correct overloaded function to call?
Constructor overloading is an example of:
A default argument in a C++ function is:
options: A value automatically assigned to a parameter if the caller does not provide one
A mandatory value the caller must always supply
A value that changes randomly each call
Only allowed for the first parameter

questions.q: In a function declaration, default arguments must generally be specified:
options: Starting from the leftmost parameters and moving right, with no gaps after a default begins
From right to left, meaning trailing parameters must have defaults before non-trailing ones

questions.q: Given void func(int a, int b=10, int c=20);, which call is valid?
If a function has default arguments, the caller:
options: May omit trailing arguments to use their default values
Must call it with zero arguments only

questions.q: Default arguments are typically specified in:
options: The function definition only, never the declaration
The function declaration/prototype (and not repeated in the definition)
Both declaration and definition identically each time

questions.q: Providing default arguments can help reduce the need for:
An inline function in C++ is a request to the compiler to:
options: Allocate the function on the heap
Replace the function call with the function's actual code at the call site
Always execute the function at compile time
Convert the function into a macro literally

questions.q: Inline functions are typically used for:
options: Small, frequently called functions to reduce function call overhead
Functions with many local variables always

questions.q: Which keyword is used to declare an inline function?
Excessive use of inline functions can lead to:
options: Increased code size due to code duplication at each call site
Slower compilation with no other effect
Removal of function overhead entirely with no cost

questions.q: The compiler may ignore the inline request and treat the function as a normal function when:
options: The function is too complex or recursive
The function is a member function

questions.q: Compared to macros, inline functions offer the advantage of:
The new operator in C++ is used to:
options: Dynamically allocate memory on the heap
Allocate memory on the stack only

questions.q: The delete operator is used to:
To dynamically allocate an array of 10 integers, the correct syntax is:
To free an array allocated with new[], the correct syntax is:
Failing to call delete on memory allocated with new results in:
Compared to malloc(), the new operator:
options: Is identical to malloc in every way

questions.q: What does the delete operator do to a pointer's value after freeing the memory?
options: Automatically sets the pointer to NULL
Does not automatically set it to NULL, leaving it dangling unless done manually
Deletes the pointer variable itself from memory

questions.q: Mixing malloc()/free() with new/delete for the same memory block is:
options: Undefined behavior and should be avoided
The standard way to manage memory in C++

questions.q: The this pointer in C++ is:
options: A pointer available in static member functions only
An implicit pointer available in non-static member functions that points to the calling object

questions.q: The this pointer allows a member function to:
options: Refer to the specific object instance that invoked the function

questions.q: In which type of member function is the this pointer NOT available?
The expression return *this; inside a member function typically:
options: Returns a pointer to the object
Returns a reference to the current object, often used for method chaining

questions.q: The this pointer is passed to member functions:
What type is the this pointer within a non-const member function of class Foo?
options: A pointer to the class type (Foo*)

questions.q: A friend function in C++ is a function that:
options: Is a member of the class
Is not a member of the class but has access to its private and protected members
Must be declared inside another class

questions.q: Which keyword is used to declare a friend function?
A friend function is declared:
options: Inside the class body with the friend keyword, but it is not a member function

questions.q: When class B is declared as a friend class of class A, it means:
options: Class A can access private members of class B only
Class B can access private and protected members of class A
Both classes lose access to each other's private members
Class B becomes a member of class A

questions.q: Is friendship in C++ mutual (i.e., if A declares B as a friend, is A automatically a friend of B)?
options: No, friendship is one-directional unless explicitly declared both ways
Only for friend classes, not friend functions

questions.q: Is friendship inherited by derived classes in C++?
A common use case for friend functions is:
options: Allowing operator overloading functions to access private data of a class

questions.q: A static data member of a class:
options: Has a separate copy for each object of the class
Is shared among all objects of the class
Cannot be accessed by any object
Is destroyed when the first object is destroyed

questions.q: A static data member must typically be defined:
options: Outside the class definition (in addition to declaration inside the class) to allocate storage
Never, as it is allocated automatically without any definition

questions.q: A static member function can access:
options: Only static data members directly (not non-static ones)
Both static and non-static data members equally
Neither static nor non-static data members

questions.q: Static member functions can be called:
options: Only through an object of the class
Using the class name directly, without needing an object
Only from within the class's own member functions

questions.q: Does a static member function have access to the this pointer?
options: No, because it is not associated with any particular object

questions.q: A static local variable inside a function:
options: Is reinitialized every time the function is called
Retains its value between function calls
Is destroyed after each function call

questions.q: Which of the following is true about a static member shared across objects?
options: Each object gets its own independent copy
All objects of the class share a single copy of that member
Static members cannot be modified after compilation
Static members require dynamic memory allocation

questions.q: Declaring a variable with const means:
options: Its value can be changed anytime
Its value cannot be modified after initialization
It is stored only in the heap

questions.q: A const member function in a class:
options: Can modify any data member of the object
Promises not to modify the data members of the object (except mutable ones)
Can only be called on non-const objects
Is the same as a static member function

questions.q: Which of the following correctly declares a const pointer to an int (the pointer itself cannot change, but the value it points to can)?
Which of the following declares a pointer to a const int (the value pointed to cannot change through this pointer, but the pointer itself can point elsewhere)?
Calling a non-const member function on a const object is:
options: Not allowed, since it may modify the object's state

questions.q: A const object can only call:
options: Any member function of the class
Const member functions of the class

questions.q: Which keyword allows a specific data member to be modified even inside a const member function?
Passing a large object to a function as a const reference (const Type&) is commonly done to:
options: Allow the function to modify the object
Avoid copying the object while preventing the function from modifying it
Force a deep copy of the object every time
Make the object a static member

questions.q: Exception handling in C++ primarily uses which three keywords?
Code that might raise an exception is placed inside a:
options: finally block (C++ has no finally block)

questions.q: The throw keyword is used to:
A catch block with ellipsis (catch(...)) is used to:
options: Catch a specific exception type only

questions.q: If no matching catch block is found for a thrown exception, the program:
Which statement re-throws the currently caught exception from within a catch block?
C++ exception handling is primarily useful for:
options: Separating error-handling code from normal program logic and handling runtime errors gracefully

questions.q: Can a try block have multiple catch blocks?
options: No, only one catch block is allowed per try block
Yes, multiple catch blocks can handle different exception types thrown from the same try block
Only two catch blocks are allowed

questions.q: A function template in C++ allows:
options: Writing a single function definition that works with multiple data types
Writing multiple functions with the same name and same type only

questions.q: Which keyword is used to declare a template?
In template<typename T> or template<class T>, the keywords typename and class in this context are:
options: Generally interchangeable as a way to declare a template type parameter
Used only for classes, never functions

questions.q: A class template allows:
options: Creating a blueprint for a class that can operate on generic data types
Only one instantiation of the class ever

questions.q: The process of creating a specific version of a template for a given type (e.g., Stack<int>) is called:
Template specialization allows:
options: Providing a custom implementation of a template for a specific data type
Preventing a template from being instantiated
Converting a template into a macro

questions.q: Compared to function overloading, function templates:
options: Require writing separate code for each data type
Let the compiler generate type-specific code from a single generic definition
Cannot work with built-in data types

questions.q: Templates in C++ are primarily processed:
options: At compile time, generating code for each type used

questions.q: std::vector is an example of:
options: A class template (template class) from the STL

sections.name: STL Basics (vector, list, map, set, stack, queue, iterators)

questions.q: The Standard Template Library (STL) in C++ primarily provides:
options: Generic, reusable data structures and algorithms like containers, iterators, and algorithms

questions.q: Which STL container stores elements in contiguous memory and allows dynamic resizing, similar to a dynamic array?
Which STL container is implemented as a doubly linked list, allowing efficient insertion/deletion at any position but no direct random access?
A std::map in the STL stores elements as:
options: Key-value pairs, typically sorted by key

questions.q: A std::set in the STL stores:
options: Unique elements, typically maintained in sorted order

questions.q: Which STL container follows Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) ordering?
Which STL container follows First-In-First-Out (FIFO) ordering?
In the STL, an iterator is best described as:
options: A function that sorts a container
An object that allows traversal through the elements of a container, similar in concept to a pointer
